questions.question: In a picture of steady flow past an airfoil, the streamlines above it are drawn closer together than far ahead of it. What does that tell you about the air between them?
options: It moves faster there, because the same flow passes through a narrower stream tube
It moves slower there, because crowded streamlines mean the air is piling up
It is denser there, because the streamlines are packed more tightly
Nothing, because the spacing of streamlines is chosen freely when drawing them
questions.explanation: No fluid crosses a streamline, so the space between two streamlines is a stream tube carrying a fixed flow. Where the tube narrows, continuity makes the speed rise. In steady flow nothing piles up, the low-speed air keeps its density, and in a drawing like this the spacing does carry meaning.

questions.question: Water flows at 6 m/s in a pipe of 10 cm diameter that narrows to 5 cm diameter. What is the speed in the narrow part?
options: 24 m/s
12 m/s
3 m/s
questions.explanation: Water is incompressible, so A1V1 = A2V2. The area goes with the square of the diameter: halving the diameter quarters the area, so the speed is 4 × 6 = 24 m/s. 12 m/s uses the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio; 1.5 m/s and 3 m/s turn the ratio upside down.

questions.question: Euler's equation, dp = −ρV dV, applies along a streamline. A fluid element moves into a region where the flow is faster. What happens to the pressure it feels?
options: It falls: a rise in speed comes with a fall in pressure
It rises: faster air pushes harder on everything around it
It stays the same: speed and pressure are independent
It falls only if the density also falls
questions.explanation: With dV > 0 the minus sign makes dp < 0. The element speeds up because the pressure ahead of it is lower: the pressure difference pushes it forward. The derivation did not need the density to change.

questions.question: In which case may Bernoulli's equation, p + ½ρV² = constant, be applied between the two points named?
options: Two points on one streamline in steady air flow at 40 m/s, far from any surface
A point ahead of a propeller and a point in its slipstream behind it
Two points on one streamline in air flow at 400 m/s
Two points inside the thin layer of air rubbing along a wing surface
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's equation needs steady, incompressible flow without friction and with no energy added between the points. A propeller adds energy, air at 400 m/s is compressible (well above 100 m/s), and friction acts in the thin layer next to a surface.

questions.question: A water U-tube manometer is connected between two points of an air duct and reads h = 3.0 cm. What is the pressure difference between the two points? (Use g = 9.8 m/s².)
options: 294 Pa
30 Pa
questions.explanation: Δp = ρLgh with the density of the manometer liquid, water, and h in meters: 1,000 × 9.8 × 0.030 = 294 Pa. 0.36 Pa uses the density of air, 29,400 Pa keeps h in centimeters, and 30 Pa leaves out g.

questions.question: An aircraft flies where the air density is 0.82 kg/m³. Its pitot-static tube measures p0 − p = 1,640 Pa. What is its true airspeed?
questions.explanation: V = √(2(p0 − p)/ρ) = √(2 × 1,640/0.82) = 63.2 m/s. 51.7 m/s uses the sea-level density, 1.2250 kg/m³ (that is the indicated airspeed); 44.7 m/s leaves out the factor 2; 4,000 m/s forgets the square root.

questions.question: What does the vertical speed indicator sense?
options: How fast the static pressure is changing
The difference between the total and the static pressure
The total pressure from the pitot tube
The value of the static pressure itself
questions.explanation: Its diaphragm is fed straight from the static line and its case through a calibrated leak, so a difference appears only while the static pressure is changing: in a climb or a descent. The difference between total and static pressure drives the airspeed indicator, and the value of the static pressure drives the altimeter.

questions.question: Ice blocks the static port of an airplane while the pitot tube stays clear. Once the airplane changes altitude, which instruments read wrong?
options: The airspeed indicator, the altimeter, and the vertical speed indicator
Only the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator
Only the airspeed indicator
None of them, because the pitot tube is still clear
questions.explanation: The static line feeds all three instruments. The trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter and holds the vertical speed indicator at zero, and the airspeed indicator, which compares the total pressure with that trapped static pressure, reads low in a climb and high in a descent. Forgetting that the airspeed indicator also uses the static line leaves it off the list.
